summary:
TeraTrend is a web application that tells farmers and planners whether any location in India is good for agriculture, and whether that is changing. Enter a place or click the map, and TeraTrend analyses two decades of NASA Earth observation data (GLDAS, MERRA-2, GPM, MODIS, AIRS and OMI) together with soil data. It rates temperature, moisture, soil pH, soil quality and climate as Good, Moderate or Poor.

To separate real change from normal weather noise, it applies the Hamed-Rao Modified Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope, and reports a shift only when it is statistically significant (p < 0.05). It also compares independent datasets to show how strongly each trend is supported.

TeraTrend then ranks suitable crops and estimates yield, cost, profit, ROI and risk of loss using official Indian price and cost data, along with practical soil and climate improvement advice. All results are indicative and meant to support, not replace, local expert guidance.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

TeraTrend answers two questions for any location in India: “Is this land good for farming?” and “Is that changing?”

A user clicks the map or searches for a place. The app snaps the point to a ~27 km grid cell and checks it against India’s official boundary. It then rates five factors (temperature, moisture, soil pH, soil quality and climate) as Good, Moderate or Poor, each with a score and a plain-language reason.

The data comes from six NASA datasets (GLDAS, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, MODIS, AIRS and OMI) plus the Harmonized World Soil Database hosted by NASA’s ORNL DAAC. We process them offline into compact regional files, so queries are answered in milliseconds.

To detect real change, TeraTrend aggregates monthly records into yearly values and runs the Hamed-Rao Modified Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope. These handle seasonality and year-to-year autocorrelation. A shift is reported only when it is statistically significant (p < 0.05). Otherwise the app says conditions are stable and advises against reacting to one bad season. It also compares independent datasets to show how strongly each trend is supported.

Finally, it ranks suitable crops and estimates yield, cost, profit, ROI, break-even point and risk of loss, using official Indian cost, MSP and market price data.

What are the benefits?

  • It turns raw scientific data into a clear verdict a farmer can read in seconds.
  • It prevents panic decisions, like switching crops after one drought year.
  • It warns early about slow, proven shifts, such as long-term soil-moisture decline.
  • It combines agronomy and economics, so the answer to “what should I grow?” includes “will it pay?”
  • It gives practical improvement actions (for example, lime for acidic soil) and shows the evidence and confidence behind every result.

What is the intended impact?

We want evidence-based, climate-resilient farming decisions to be accessible to smallholder farmers, extension workers and regional planners. Better crop choices can protect incomes and water resources. Planners can identify where conditions are slowly deteriorating before it becomes a crisis. Over time, the same approach can be extended to more regions and crops.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: Flask, Xarray, NumPy, Pandas, PyMannKendall, SQLAlchemy with SQLite, Shapely.
  • NASA tools: earthaccess, harmony-py, python-cmr and OPeNDAP, for authenticated access and server-side subsetting.
  • Frontend: Tailwind CSS, Leaflet.js (map) and Chart.js (trend charts).
  • Development: Git, pytest, and AI-assisted coding (Google Antigravity IDE and Claude), with all output reviewed by the team.
  • Hardware: standard personal computers. No special hardware was needed because the heavy processing is done once offline.

How is it creative?

  • It goes beyond showing data layers: it judges the land and tells users what to do.
  • It uses statistical proof as a gate, so the app is honest about “no significant change.”
  • It cross-checks six independent NASA products and reports consensus, so users see how reliable each trend is.
  • It links climate science directly to farm economics, including a probability-of-loss estimate and a 10-year outlook.
  • It is designed for accessibility: color-blind-safe charts, icons with every rating, and plans for Hindi and mobile-first use.

What factors did we consider?

  • Scientific rigor: autocorrelation, seasonality, minimum record length, and dataset traceability (DOIs and checksums recorded).
  • Data limits: the ~27 km cell is an average, no satellite measures soil pH directly, and monthly data cannot capture daily extremes. We state these limits openly and recommend local soil tests.
  • India coverage: all states and union territories, including islands and disputed-boundary regions as officially depicted, with fallbacks where land models have gaps.
  • Economic honesty: costs and prices come only from official sources, yield estimates are labeled indicative, and nothing is invented when data is missing.
  • Usability and trust: plain language, confidence levels, visible data dates, and clear disclaimers that results support, not replace, expert advice.
  • Performance and privacy: data held in memory for speed, with no personal data collected.
